summary.text: The Solar System is the Sun and the masses bound to it by gravity, most prominently its eight planets, of which Earth is one.
It formed about 4.6 billion years ago when a dense region of a molecular cloud collapsed, creating the Sun and a disc that built the planets.
The Sun holds 99.86% of the total mass, and the next most massive objects are the eight planets.

items.prompt: Astronomers find a body with planetary mass that circles the Sun directly but does not dominate its orbit. What is it?

options.label: A dwarf planet
A full planet
A moon
An asteroid-sized small body

items.explain: Objects of planetary mass that orbit the Sun directly without dominating their orbit are dwarf planets. Planets dominate their orbits, and small bodies are less massive.

options.label: Venus and Earth
Earth and Mars
Mars and Jupiter
Mercury and Venus

items.explain: Earth and Mars are the only planets that orbit within the Sun's habitable zone.

items.prompt: Imagine you set the Sun aside and weigh everything else that orbits it. Where does nearly all of that mass sit?

options.label: In the four rocky inner planets
Spread evenly across all eight planets
In Jupiter and Saturn
In the asteroid belt and comets

items.explain: Jupiter and Saturn possess nearly 90% of the non-stellar mass of the Solar System.

items.prompt: A student compares the two largest moons with the smallest planet. What does she find?

options.label: The moons are larger across but less massive
Every moon is smaller and lighter
Both moons are larger and more massive
The moons and the planet match in size

items.explain: Ganymede and Titan are larger than Mercury, though less massive.

items.prompt: A probe tracks the stream of charged particles flowing outward from the Sun. What happens to it around 70-90 AU out?

options.label: It speeds up once the planets are behind it
It is scattered by the Oort cloud's comets
It circles back toward the Sun's surface
The interstellar medium halts it, forming the heliopause

items.explain: At around 70-90 AU the solar wind is halted by the interstellar medium, giving the heliopause and the border of interstellar space.

items.prompt: A huge slowly turning gas cloud collapses under its own gravity. What does it do as it shrinks?

options.label: It spins faster and flattens into a disc around a hot centre
It stays round and spins at the same rate
It spins slower as its mass spreads outward
It splits into many equal clouds that drift apart

items.explain: As the cloud collapsed, conservation of angular momentum made it rotate faster, the centre grew hotter, and it flattened into a protoplanetary disc.

steps.text: The Sun holds 99.86% of the system's mass.
The eight planets are the next most massive objects.

paragraphs.heading: The Sun and its family
paragraphs.text: The Solar System is the Sun together with everything that gravity binds to it and that orbits it, above all its eight planets, one of which is Earth. It is a planetary system with a single star, not part of a larger star system, and it lies inside the Milky Way Galaxy. The Sun dominates it, holding 99.86% of all the mass. Next in mass come the eight planets; by definition, each one dominates its own orbit.

paragraphs.heading: Rocky worlds and giants
paragraphs.text: Nearest the Sun are the four terrestrial planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, which make up the inner Solar System. Earth and Mars are the only planets in the Sun's habitable zone, where sunlight is enough to keep water on the surface liquid under atmospheric pressure. Past the frost line, at about five astronomical units (AU), lie the outer planets: the gas giants Jupiter and Saturn and the ice giants Uranus and Neptune. Jupiter and Saturn alone carry nearly 90% of the mass that is not in the Sun.

paragraphs.heading: Dwarf planets and small bodies
paragraphs.text: Some bodies have planetary mass and orbit the Sun directly but do not dominate their orbits; these are dwarf planets. The Minor Planet Center of the International Astronomical Union lists five, Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Makemake and Haumea, and four more, Orcus, Quaoar, Gonggong and Sedna, are generally counted too. Smaller still are huge numbers of small Solar System bodies: asteroids, comets, centaurs and meteoroids, plus clouds of dust. Ceres and many small bodies sit in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, while the other dwarf planets are trans-Neptunian objects, found in the Kuiper belt just past Neptune or in the more distant scattered disc.

paragraphs.heading: Moons
paragraphs.text: Many objects circle a larger body instead of the Sun; these natural satellites are usually called moons. They range from moons of planetary mass down to tiny moonlets. The two largest, Ganymede at Jupiter and Titan at Saturn, are bigger than Mercury, the smallest planet, though they have less mass. The seven most massive moons, Earth's Moon among them, are both heavier and bigger than any dwarf planet.

paragraphs.heading: How it formed
paragraphs.text: About 4.6 billion years ago the system took shape, when a dense patch of a molecular cloud collapsed under gravity. Most of that cloud was hydrogen; the rest was some helium plus a little of the heavier elements forged by earlier generations of stars. As it collapsed it spun faster and flattened into a disc about 200 AU wide, with a hot, dense protostar at the centre. Dust and gas in the disc pulled on each other and clumped into ever larger bodies, a process called accretion. Hundreds of protoplanets may have formed, but they merged, were destroyed or were thrown out, leaving the planets, dwarf planets and smaller leftovers.

paragraphs.heading: Where it ends
paragraphs.text: Within the heliosphere, the space between the planets is filled by the solar wind, a stream of charged plasma particles, along with dust, gas and cosmic rays. At around 70–90 AU from the Sun, the interstellar medium halts the solar wind, which marks the heliopause, the border with interstellar space. Farther out, the theorized Oort cloud, the source of long-period comets, begins somewhere beyond 2,000 AU. Its outer limit is the edge of the Sun's Hill sphere, 178,000–227,000 AU away, where the Sun's gravitational potential equals that of the galaxy. The nearest star, Proxima Centauri, lies 269,000 AU (4.25 light-years) away.
